# Exercise 6: Swiss Health Model {.unnumbered}

This exercise applies the parametric kernels from the [chapter on hybrid models](../chapters/hybrid-models.qmd) to a concrete example: a model of six Swiss health variables relating lifestyle factors to disease risk and healthcare costs. We proceed in three stages: first exploring each regression kernel individually, then writing the complete model, and finally conditioning on observed evidence. To foreshadow the [next chapter](../chapters/intervening.qmd), we include cases that preview the distinction between *observing* and *forcing* a variable.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Prerequisites: Python libraries"}
This exercise uses the following libraries:

- [**WeightedSampling.torch**](../appendix/WeightedSampling.qmd) — for probabilistic programming and inference. Install via:
  ```bash
  pip install git+https://github.com/MariusFurter/WeightedSampling.torch.git
  ```
- [**PyTorch**](https://pytorch.org/) — for tensor operations. A short tutorial can be found in the [Appendix](../appendix/pytorch.qmd).
- [**matplotlib**](https://matplotlib.org/) — for plotting.

If any packages are missing, run `pip install torch matplotlib` in your terminal.
:::

## The model

The model relates six variables:

| Variable | Symbol | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Smoking status | $S$ | $\{0,1\}$ |
| Age | $A$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ |
| Physical activity | $P$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ |
| BMI | $B$ | $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ |
| Diabetes | $D$ | $\{0,1\}$ |
| Healthcare costs | $C$ | $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ |

Smoking status, age, and physical activity are root variables with no parents. Together they influence BMI through a linear regression kernel. BMI and age jointly determine diabetes risk through a logistic regression kernel. Finally, diabetes status, smoking status, and BMI jointly determine healthcare costs through a log-normal regression kernel. BMI appears as a parent of both $D$ and $C$; age appears as a parent of both $B$ and $D$; smoking appears as a parent of both $B$ and $C$.

``` {.tikz file="exercises/swiss-health-model.tikz"}
%%| label: fig-swiss-health-model
%%| fig-cap: String diagram for the Swiss health model.
%%| height: 10em
```

The parameters below are grounded in publicly available Swiss summary statistics. Where a parameter corresponds to a published statistic we read its value directly; where possible, we derive regression coefficients from published relative risks. The remaining coefficients are calibrated so that the model's marginal distributions reproduce published target values.

## Data sources

- **BFS Gesundheit — Taschenstatistik 2025** (based on the Swiss Health Survey, SGB 2022): smoking prevalence (p. 20), overweight and obesity rates (pp. 20–21), diabetes prevalence (pp. 8–9), physical activity (p. 20), doctor consultations (p. 31), and healthcare costs (p. 32).
- **Obsan Bericht 10/2020: Diabetes Mellitus** (Fürst & Probst-Hensch, 2020): disease burden and care in Switzerland. Reference data include diabetes prevalence by age and data source (ch. 8), BMI $\geq$ 25 prevalence among diabetics (SAPALDIA: 79–83% vs. 50–56% among non-diabetics, p. 49), and direct healthcare costs for diabetic patients (CHF 8,239/year, Helsana 2011, p. 47).
- **Kosten von nichtübertragbaren Krankheiten in der Schweiz** (Stucki et al., 2025, ZHAW/Uni Luzern/BFH for BAG): full NCD cost report (156 pp.). Relative risks for diabetes type 2 from overweight: RR = 2.25 (M) / 2.30 (F); from obesity: RR = 5.50 (M) / 7.00 (F) (Tables 20–21, from Lobstein & Leach, 2010). Physical inactivity relative risk for diabetes: RR = 1.17 (Kyu et al., 2016). For obesity: OR = 1.49 (Bell et al., 2014, Table 28). Total healthcare costs attributable to overweight/obesity: CHF 3.7 billion (2022), of which diabetes type 2 accounts for CHF 1.07 billion, with an additional CHF 2.9 billion in productivity losses (Tables 22–25). 150,315 DALYs (Table 26), of which diabetes type 2 accounts for 58,293 (39%).
- **CoLaus study** (Kaiser et al., 2012, *Diabetic Medicine* 29: 190–197): population-based study of 6,188 subjects (35–75 years) in Lausanne. Multivariable-adjusted odds ratios for type 2 diabetes (Table 4): BMI overweight OR = 1.51 (1.07–2.12), obese OR = 5.14 (3.39–7.78); physical activity OR = 0.64 (0.51–0.80); age 65–75 vs. 35–44 OR = 8.20 (5.22–12.9). T2D prevalence 6.3%; mean BMI of diabetics 30.2 vs. 25.5 for non-diabetics.
- **Sport Schweiz 2020** (BASPO / Lamprecht & Stamm): physical activity categories and sport behavior (pp. 12–16).
- **WHO Global Health Observatory**: mean BMI by country (age-standardized).
- **IDF Diabetes Atlas**: diabetes prevalence by country.
- **OECD Health at a Glance (2023)**: doctor consultations per capita.
- **BFS Population Statistics (STATPOP)**: median age and age distribution.
- **Dare et al. (2015)** (*BMJ Open* 5: e008330): cross-sectional study showing current smokers have BMI roughly 0.3–0.7 kg/m² lower than non-smokers.

### Root distributions

The three root variables are specified by marginal distributions (kernels $I \kernel X$ with trivial input):

- **Smoking** $S \sim \mathsf{Bernoulli}(0.24)$. BFS Taschenstatistik 2025 / SGB 2022 reports 27% (men) and 21% (women); we use the average $0.24$.
- **Age** $A \sim \mathsf{Gamma}(6,\, \tfrac{6}{43})$, with mean $43$ and standard deviation $\approx 17.5$. The Gamma approximates the right-skewed adult age distribution; BFS-reported median ages are 41.9 years (men) and 44.0 years (women), giving a combined median of $\approx 43$ years.
- **Physical activity** $P \sim \mathsf{Gamma}(1.60,\, 0.42)$, with mean $\approx 3.8$ and standard deviation $\approx 3.0$, measured in hours of sport per week. Parameters moment-matched to the Sport Schweiz 2020 weekly hours distribution (never 16%, <2h 10%, 2h 15%, 3–4h 25%, 5–6h 16%, 7+h 18%) using all six category midpoints 0, 1, 2, 3.5, 5.5, and 9 hours. Note: the Gamma distribution has support $(0,\infty)$ and cannot represent the 16% point mass at $P=0$; the fitted distribution approximates but underweights the never-exerciser group.

## Part 0: Visualizing the root distributions {#sec-roots}

Before building the regression kernels, it is useful to visualize the three root distributions to develop intuition for the range of inputs the model will encounter.

**Task 0 — Plot the root distributions.**

Write `@model root_distributions()` that samples $S$, $A$, $P$ from their respective root distributions. Run with 10,000 particles and produce a figure with three panels:

1. A bar chart of $S$ showing $P(S=0)$ and $P(S=1)$.
2. A histogram of $A$ with the theoretical $\mathsf{Gamma}(6,\, \tfrac{6}{43})$ density overlaid. Use `torch.linspace` to create a grid of values and `dist.Gamma(...).log_prob(grid).exp()` to compute the density.
3. A histogram of $P$ with the theoretical $\mathsf{Gamma}(1.60,\, 0.42)$ density overlaid.

Bonus: Look up the actual age distribution of Swiss adults. How does this compare to the Gamma distribution used in the model?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def root_distributions():
    S = sample("S", dist.Bernoulli(0.24))
    A = sample("A", dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0/43.0))
    P = sample("P", dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42))

result_roots = root_distributions(num_particles=10_000)
S_vals = result_roots["S"]
A_vals = result_roots["A"]
P_vals = result_roots["P"]
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))

# S: bar chart
axes[0].bar([0, 1],
            [(S_vals == 0).float().mean().item(), (S_vals == 1).float().mean().item()],
            color=["steelblue", "darkorange"], width=0.5)
axes[0].set_xticks([0, 1])
axes[0].set_xticklabels(["S = 0\n(non-smoker)", "S = 1\n(smoker)"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Proportion")
axes[0].set_title("Smoking status $S$")
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1)

# A: histogram + theoretical density
A_grid = torch.linspace(1e-3, 120, 500)
A_density = dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0 / 43.0).log_prob(A_grid).exp()
axes[1].hist(A_vals.numpy(), bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.5, color="steelblue")
axes[1].plot(A_grid.numpy(), A_density.numpy(), color="steelblue", linewidth=2)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Age (years)")
axes[1].set_title("Age $A \\sim \\mathrm{Gamma}(6,\\, \\frac{6}{43})$")

# P: histogram + theoretical density
P_grid = torch.linspace(1e-3, 15, 500)
P_density = dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42).log_prob(P_grid).exp()
axes[2].hist(P_vals.numpy(), bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.5, color="darkorange")
axes[2].plot(P_grid.numpy(), P_density.numpy(), color="darkorange", linewidth=2)
axes[2].set_xlabel("Hours of sport per week")
axes[2].set_title("Physical activity $P \\sim \\mathrm{Gamma}(1.60,\\, 0.42)$")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The actual age distribution is flatter on and has several plateaus. In particular, the Gamma approximation vastly underestimates the number of young people. A more accurate mode could use a custom distribution fitted to the empirical age distribution.

:::

## Part 1: Regression kernels {#sec-kernels}

In this part we explore each regression kernel by writing a small `@model` that samples the relevant inputs and applies the kernel. In Part 2 we will combine all three into a single model.

### 1.1 BMI kernel (linear regression) {#sec-bmi-task}

BMI depends on all three root variables via a linear regression kernel with linear predictor
$$B \mid S, A, P \sim \mathsf{Normal}(\eta_B, \sigma^2), \qquad \eta_B = \alpha_0 + \alpha_S S + \alpha_A A + \alpha_P P$$

Although BMI is positive, the Normal distribution is used here as a standard modeling approximation; with the calibrated parameters, fewer than 0.1% of samples fall below zero.

**Task 1 — BMI kernel.**

Write `@model bmi_model(S_val, A_val, P_val)` that takes fixed values for $S$, $A$, $P$ as arguments and samples $B$ from the linear regression kernel using $\alpha_0 = 25.0$, $\alpha_S = -0.5$, $\alpha_A = 0.05$, $\alpha_P = -0.3$, $\sigma = 3.8$. Then answer the following:

a. Run with typical values $S=0$, $A=42$, $P=5$ and 10,000 particles. Plot the distribution of $B$ and compute the sample mean. What does the predictor formula give for $\mu$?
b. What happens to $\mu$ when $S$ changes from $0$ to $1$, with $A=42$ and $P=5$ fixed? First predict from the formula, then verify numerically.
c. What happens to $\mu$ when $A$ increases by $20$, from $42$ to $62$, with $S=0$ and $P=5$ fixed? Predict, then verify.
d. Consider a 65-year-old smoker with low physical activity: $S=1$, $A=65$, $P=1$. Compute $\mu$ directly, verify numerically, and express the total shift from the baseline $(S=0, A=42, P=5)$ as a sum of three individual contributions.
e. What would happen to $\mu$ if $\alpha_A$ were doubled to $0.10$ (with $S=0$, $A=42$, $P=5$)? Predict from the formula, then verify by running a modified model.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Plug both sets of values into the predictor formula and compute the difference.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Key observation.** The Normal distribution is parametrized directly by its mean, so $\mathbb{E}[B \mid S, A, P] = \mu = \eta_B$. Hence, the linear predictor *is* the conditional expectation. This is a special property of the Normal. As a consequence, changing one input by $\Delta$ while holding all others fixed shifts $\mu$ by exactly $\alpha \cdot \Delta$: each coefficient is the *rate of change of the mean per unit increase in that variable, with all other variables held constant*.

---

**Part a.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def bmi_model(S_val, A_val, P_val):
    eta_B = 25.0 + (-0.5) * S_val + 0.05 * A_val + (-0.3) * P_val
    B = sample("B", dist.Normal(eta_B, 3.8))

result_base = bmi_model(0.0, 42.0, 5.0, num_particles=10_000)
B_base = result_base["B"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(B_base.numpy(), bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.7, color="steelblue")
ax.axvline(B_base.mean().item(), color="red", linewidth=1.5,
           label=f"mean = {B_base.mean():.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("BMI ($B$)")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Sample mean E[B | S=0, A=42, P=5] = {B_base.mean():.2f}")
```

The predictor gives $\mu = 25.0 + (-0.5)\cdot 0 + 0.05\cdot 42 + (-0.3)\cdot 5 = 25.6$; the sample mean should be close.

---

**Part b.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_smoker = bmi_model(1.0, 42.0, 5.0, num_particles=10_000)

print(f"E[B | S=0]: {B_base.mean():.2f}")
print(f"E[B | S=1]: {result_smoker['B'].mean():.2f}")
print(f"Shift:      {result_smoker['B'].mean() - B_base.mean():.3f}  (predicted: α_S = -0.5)")
```

The shift in $\mu$ is exactly $\alpha_S = -0.5$: going from non-smoker to smoker decreases $\mu$ — and hence $\mathbb{E}[B]$ — by $0.5$ BMI units, with $A$ and $P$ held fixed.

---

**Part c.**

The predicted shift is $\alpha_A \cdot \Delta A = 0.05 \times 20 = +1.0$.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_older = bmi_model(0.0, 62.0, 5.0, num_particles=10_000)

print(f"E[B | A=42]: {B_base.mean():.3f}")
print(f"E[B | A=62]: {result_older['B'].mean():.3f}")
print(f"Shift:       {result_older['B'].mean() - B_base.mean():.3f}  (predicted: +1.0)")
```

The total effect scales linearly with $\Delta A$: 20 years at $\alpha_A = 0.05$ gives $+1.0$.

---

**Part d.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
mu_highrisk = 25.0 + (-0.5)*1 + 0.05*65 + (-0.3)*1
print(f"Predicted μ = 25.0 + (-0.5)·1 + 0.05·65 + (-0.3)·1 = {mu_highrisk:.2f}")

result_highrisk = bmi_model(1.0, 65.0, 1.0, num_particles=10_000)
print(f"E[B | S=1, A=65, P=1] = {result_highrisk['B'].mean():.2f}  (predicted: {mu_highrisk:.2f})")

total_shift = (-0.5)*1 + 0.05*(65-42) + (-0.3)*(1-5)
print(f"\nShift from baseline: α_S·ΔS + α_A·ΔA + α_P·ΔP")
print(f"  = (-0.5)·1 + 0.05·23 + (-0.3)·(-4) = {total_shift:.2f}")
```

The shifts decompose as: smoking $(-0.5)$, older age $(+1.15)$, lower activity $(+1.2)$, for a combined $+1.85$ above baseline.

---

**Part e.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
predicted_alpha_shift = (0.10 - 0.05) * 42.0
print(f"Predicted shift: +{predicted_alpha_shift:.2f} BMI units")

@model
def bmi_model_alt(S_val, A_val, P_val):
    eta_B = 25.0 + (-0.5) * S_val + 0.10 * A_val + (-0.3) * P_val  # α_A doubled
    B = sample("B", dist.Normal(eta_B, 3.8))

result_alt = bmi_model_alt(0.0, 42.0, 5.0, num_particles=10_000)

print(f"E[B] (α_A=0.05): {B_base.mean():.2f}")
print(f"E[B] (α_A=0.10): {result_alt['B'].mean():.2f}")
print(f"Shift: {result_alt['B'].mean() - B_base.mean():.2f}  (predicted: +{predicted_alpha_shift:.2f})")
```

Changing a coefficient rescales its variable's contribution to $\eta_B$: $\mu$ shifts by exactly the change in the predictor value at the current inputs, $\Delta\alpha_A \times A = 0.05 \times 42 = 2.1$.

:::

### 1.2 Diabetes kernel (logistic regression) {#sec-diabetes-task}

Diabetes depends on BMI and age via a logistic regression kernel:
$$
D \mid B, A \;\sim\; \mathsf{Bernoulli}\bigl(\sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1\, B + \beta_2\, A)\bigr), \qquad \sigma(x) = \tfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
$$

**Task 2 — Diabetes kernel.**

Write `@model diabetes_model(B_val, A_val)` that takes fixed BMI and age values and samples $D$ from the logistic regression kernel using $\beta_0 = -9.6$, $\beta_1 = 0.15$, and $\beta_2 = 0.07$. Then answer the following:

a. Run with $B_{\mathsf{val}} = 25$ and $B_{\mathsf{val}} = 30$ at typical age $A_{\mathsf{val}} = 42$ using 10,000 particles each. For each, compute the fraction of samples with $D=1$ and compare to the formula $P(D=1 \mid B, A) = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 B + \beta_2 A)$.
b. Plot $P(D=1 \mid B, A)$ as a function of $B$ for three fixed ages ($A = 25$, $A = 42$, $A = 65$) in two panels:

  - a wide view over $B \in [0, 60]$ to show the full S-shape of the sigmoid
  - a zoomed view over $B \in [15, 45]$ (the realistic BMI range) where you can read off threshold BMIs at which the risk for each age group crosses 10% and 50%.

c. Looking at the plot, does a 1-unit increase in BMI always shift $P(D=1)$ by the same amount? At age $A = 42$, compute $P(D=1)$ at $B=20$ and $B=21$, and again at $B=33$ and $B=34$, and compare the two differences. What does $\beta_1 = 0.15$ actually control?
d. Fix $B = 25$ and vary age. Compute $P(D=1 \mid B=25, A=25)$ and $P(D=1 \mid B=25, A=65)$. What is the odds ratio for a 40-year increase in age? How does $\beta_2 = 0.07$ relate to the CoLaus reported OR of $8.20$ for ages 65–75 vs. 35–44?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Model.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def diabetes_model(B_val, A_val):
    eta_D = torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * B_val + 0.07 * A_val)
    D = sample("D", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(eta_D)))
```

---

**Part a.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_D25 = diabetes_model(25.0, 42.0, num_particles=10_000)
result_D30 = diabetes_model(30.0, 42.0, num_particles=10_000)

p25 = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 25.0 + 0.07 * 42.0)))
p30 = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 30.0 + 0.07 * 42.0)))

print(f"B = 25, A = 42:  formula {p25:.4f},  sample {result_D25['D'].mean():.4f}")
print(f"B = 30, A = 42:  formula {p30:.4f},  sample {result_D30['D'].mean():.4f}")
```

---

**Part b.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
B_wide = torch.linspace(0, 60, 500)
B_zoom = torch.linspace(15, 45, 300)

ages = [25.0, 42.0, 65.0]
colors = ["steelblue", "darkorange", "crimson"]

# threshold BMIs where P(D=1) = 0.1 and 0.5 for each age:
# σ(β_0 + β_1 B + β_2 A) = 0.1  ⟹  B_10 = (log(0.1/0.9) + 9.6 - 0.07·A) / 0.15
# σ(β_0 + β_1 B + β_2 A) = 0.5  ⟹  B_50 = (9.6 - 0.07·A) / 0.15
B_10 = {a: (torch.log(torch.tensor(0.1 / 0.9)).item() + 9.6 - 0.07 * a) / 0.15 for a in ages}
B_50 = {a: (9.6 - 0.07 * a) / 0.15 for a in ages}
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))

for a, col in zip(ages, colors):
    p_w = torch.sigmoid(-9.6 + 0.15 * B_wide + 0.07 * a)
    p_z = torch.sigmoid(-9.6 + 0.15 * B_zoom + 0.07 * a)
    axes[0].plot(B_wide.numpy(), p_w.numpy(), color=col, linewidth=2, label=f"$A={int(a)}$")
    axes[1].plot(B_zoom.numpy(), p_z.numpy(), color=col, linewidth=2, label=f"$A={int(a)}$")
    axes[1].axvline(B_10[a], linestyle=":", color=col, linewidth=0.9)

# Left: full S-curves
axes[0].set_xlabel("BMI ($B$)")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$P(D=1 \mid B, A)$")
axes[0].set_title("Full S-curves by age")
axes[0].set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)

# Right: zoomed to realistic BMI range with thresholds and sample points
axes[1].axhline(0.1, linestyle="--", color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
axes[1].axhline(0.5, linestyle="--", color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
axes[1].scatter([25.0, 30.0],
                [result_D25["D"].mean().item(), result_D30["D"].mean().item()],
                color="black", zorder=5, s=40, label="samples ($A=42$)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("BMI ($B$)")
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$P(D=1 \mid B, A)$")
axes[1].set_title("Zoomed: realistic BMI range")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

---

**Part c.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
p20 = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 20.0 + 0.07 * 42.0)))
p21 = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 21.0 + 0.07 * 42.0)))
p33 = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 33.0 + 0.07 * 42.0)))
p34 = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 34.0 + 0.07 * 42.0)))

print(f"B=20 → 21  (A=42):  P shifts by {p21 - p20:.5f}")
print(f"B=33 → 34  (A=42):  P shifts by {p34 - p33:.5f}")
```

The shifts are very different even though both inputs change by exactly $1$. Near $B=20$ the curve is nearly flat (diabetes is so rare that an extra BMI unit barely moves the needle), while near $B=33$ — where risk is around 10–20% — the curve is much steeper.

What $\beta_1 = 0.15$ does control is how much each unit of $B$ shifts the **predictor** $\eta_D = \beta_0 + \beta_1 B + \beta_2 A$: a fixed additive shift of $+0.15$ in $\eta_D$ per BMI unit, every time, regardless of $B$ or $A$. The sigmoid then converts that predictor shift into a probability change, but this conversion is steep when $\eta_D \approx 0$ (near the 50% mark) and nearly flat when $|\eta_D|$ is large. As a result, the same coefficient $\beta_1$ produces large probability swings in the mid-risk range and tiny ones in the tails.

We can always compare $P(D=1)$ at any two BMI values directly by plugging into the formula. But $\beta_1$ does not give us a fixed "probability increase per BMI unit."

---

**Part d.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
p_young = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 25.0 + 0.07 * 25.0)))
p_old   = float(torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(-9.6 + 0.15 * 25.0 + 0.07 * 65.0)))

print(f"P(D=1 | B=25, A=25): {p_young:.4f}")
print(f"P(D=1 | B=25, A=65): {p_old:.4f}")

or_40 = torch.exp(torch.tensor(0.07 * 40)).item()
or_30 = torch.exp(torch.tensor(0.07 * 30)).item()
print(f"\nOR for 40-year increase: exp(0.07 × 40) = {or_40:.2f}")
print(f"OR for 30-year increase (CoLaus-like): exp(0.07 × 30) = {or_30:.2f}  (CoLaus: 8.20)")
```

The odds ratio for a 40-year age increase is $e^{0.07 \times 40} = e^{2.8} \approx 16.4$: fixing BMI, the odds of diabetes are about 16 times higher at age 65 than at age 25. For the CoLaus reference (age midpoints ~70 vs. ~40, a 30-year gap), the model gives $e^{0.07 \times 30} = e^{2.1} \approx 8.17$ — very close to the published OR of $8.20$. The age effect is independent of BMI: both $B$ and $A$ enter the predictor additively, so their contributions separate, and changing one variable always multiplies the odds by the same factor regardless of the other variable's value.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Interpreting logistic regression coefficients via odds" collapse="true"}
The **risk** of diabetes at a given BMI is the probability $p = P(D=1 \mid B)$. One way to quantify how that risk compares to its complement is the **odds**:
$$\text{odds}(B) = \frac{P(D=1 \mid B)}{P(D=0 \mid B)} = \frac{p}{1-p}.$$
Odds and probability carry the same information but they scale differently. A risk of 1% corresponds to odds of 1:99 ($\approx 0.01$); a risk of 50% to odds of 1:1 ($= 1$); a risk of 90% to odds of 9:1 ($= 9$).

The predictor $\eta_D = \beta_0 + \beta_1 B + \beta_2 A$ is exactly the **log-odds** (also called the **logit**) of $D=1$:
$$\eta_D = \ln\!\frac{P(D=1 \mid B, A)}{P(D=0 \mid B, A)},$$
since $\sigma(\eta) = p$ implies $\eta = \ln(p/(1-p))$. On this scale the model is linear, and each coefficient has a clean interpretation: a one-unit increase in $B$ (or $A$) adds $\beta_1$ (or $\beta_2$) to the log-odds, which is equivalent to **multiplying the odds by $e^{\beta_1}$** (or $e^{\beta_2}$). These multiplicative factors are called **odds ratios**.

For this model, $e^{\beta_1} = e^{0.15} \approx 1.16$: each additional BMI unit multiplies the odds of diabetes by $1.16$, a 16% increase in the odds, holding age fixed. Similarly, $e^{\beta_2} = e^{0.07} \approx 1.07$: each additional year of age multiplies the odds by about $1.07$, holding BMI fixed. Importantly, both multiplicative factors are constant — they do not depend on where on the S-curve you are. In contrast, the corresponding changes in risk (probability) depend on the baseline: a 16% odds increase near a baseline risk of 1% shifts probability by very little, while the same odds increase near 10% risk produces a noticeably larger absolute shift.

So the right way to read a logistic regression coefficient is: $\beta > 0$ means the covariate increases the odds of $D=1$, and $e^{\beta}$ tells you by what multiplicative factor, with all other covariates held fixed. For predictions at specific inputs, always use the full formula $\sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 B + \beta_2 A)$ directly.
:::

### 1.3 Cost kernel (log-normal regression) {#sec-cost-task}

Annual healthcare costs are strictly positive and right-skewed. They depend on diabetes status, smoking status, and BMI via a log-normal regression kernel:
$$
\log C \mid S, D, B \;\sim\; \mathsf{Normal}(\gamma_0 + \gamma_S\, S + \gamma_D\, D + \gamma_B\, B,\; \tau^2).
$$

**Task 3 — Cost kernel.**

Write `@model cost_model(S_val, D_val, B_val)` that takes fixed values for $S$, $D$, and $B$ and samples $C$ from the log-normal regression kernel using $\gamma_0 = 7.5$, $\gamma_S = 0.2$, $\gamma_D = 0.65$, $\gamma_B = 0.03$, $\tau = 0.6$.
Then answer the following:

a. Run the model twice: once with $S=0, D=0, B=25$ and once with $S=0, D=1, B=25$. Plot the two predictive distributions side by side.

**Bonus (Part b).** The **median** of a distribution is the value $m$ such that $P(X \leq m) = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Show that if $f$ is strictly monotone increasing and $m$ is the median of $X$, then $f(m)$ is the median of $f(X)$.

**Bonus (Part c).** Use Part b to derive a formula for $\mathrm{median}(C \mid S, D, B)$, recalling that $C = e^X$ with $X \sim \mathsf{Normal}(\eta_C, \tau^2)$ and that $\mathrm{median}(X) = \eta_C$. Use this formula to interpret the coefficients $\gamma_S$, $\gamma_D$, and $\gamma_B$. *Hint: Take the ratio of the median at two inputs that differ only in one variable.*

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Model.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def cost_model(S_val, D_val, B_val):
    eta_C = 7.5 + 0.2 * S_val + 0.65 * D_val + 0.03 * B_val
    C = sample("C", dist.LogNormal(eta_C, 0.6))
```

---

**Part a.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_nd = cost_model(0.0, 0.0, 25.0, num_particles=10_000)
result_d  = cost_model(0.0, 1.0, 25.0, num_particles=10_000)
C_nd = result_nd["C"]
C_d  = result_d["C"]
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, vals, label in zip(axes, [C_nd, C_d], ["D=0 (no diabetes)", "D=1 (diabetes)"]):
    ax.hist(vals.numpy(), bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_xlabel("Annual cost (CHF)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

---

**Bonus (Part b).**

Let $m$ be the median of $X$, so $P(X \leq m) = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Since $f$ is strictly increasing, $f(X) \leq f(m)$ iff $X \leq m$, so $P(f(X) \leq f(m)) = P(X \leq m) = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Hence $f(m)$ is the median of $f(X)$.

---

**Bonus (Part c).**

Applying Part b with $f = \exp$:
$$\mathrm{median}(C \mid S, D, B) = e^{\mathrm{median}(X)} = e^{\eta_C} = e^{\gamma_0 + \gamma_S S + \gamma_D D + \gamma_B B}.$$

Changing any single input while holding the others fixed multiplies the median by the corresponding exponential factor. For example, the ratio of medians at $D + \Delta$ and $D$ (with $S$ and $B$ fixed) is $e^{\gamma_D \Delta}$. In particular:
- Having diabetes ($\Delta = 1$) multiplies the median by $e^{0.65} \approx 1.92$.
- Smoking ($S: 0 \to 1$) multiplies the median by $e^{0.2} \approx 1.22$.
- Each additional BMI unit multiplies the median by $e^{0.03} \approx 1.03$.

Note that $\tau$ plays no role.
:::

## Part 2: The full model {#sec-assembly}

**Task 4 — Write and verify the full model.**

Write `@model swiss_health()` that samples all six variables in a single model:

1. Sample $S$, $A$, $P$ from their root distributions.
2. Sample $B$ from the BMI kernel (linear regression on $S$, $A$, $P$).
3. Sample $D$ from the diabetes kernel (logistic regression on $B$ and $A$).
4. Sample $C$ from the cost kernel (log-normal regression on $D$, $B$).

Run with 10,000 particles, print the `summary`, and verify that the model reproduces the following published Swiss benchmarks:

| Quantity | Target |
|---|---|
| $P(B \geq 25)$ — overweight or obese | ~43% (SGB 2022) |
| $P(B \geq 30)$ — obese | ~12% (SGB 2022) |
| $P(D = 1)$ — diabetes prevalence | ~5–7% (SGB 2022) |
| Median annual cost | ~CHF 3,300 (BFS Taschenstatistik 2025: KVG CHF 264/month + VVG CHF 68/month, adjusted for LogNormal skew) |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def swiss_health():
    S = sample("S", dist.Bernoulli(0.24))
    A = sample("A", dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0/43.0))
    P = sample("P", dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42))
    eta_B = 25.0 + (-0.5) * S + 0.05 * A + (-0.3) * P
    B = sample("B", dist.Normal(eta_B, 3.8))
    eta_D = -9.6 + 0.15 * B + 0.07 * A
    D = sample("D", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(eta_D)))
    eta_C = 7.5 + 0.2 * S + 0.65 * D + 0.03 * B
    C = sample("C", dist.LogNormal(eta_C, 0.6))

result = swiss_health(num_particles=10_000)
print(summary(result))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
B_vals = result["B"]
D_vals = result["D"]
C_vals = result["C"]

print(f"P(BMI >= 25):       {(B_vals >= 25).float().mean():.3f}   (target ~0.43)")
print(f"P(BMI >= 30):       {(B_vals >= 30).float().mean():.3f}   (target ~0.12)")
print(f"P(Diabetes = 1):    {D_vals.mean():.3f}   (target ~0.05–0.07)")
print(f"Median cost (CHF):  {C_vals.median().item():,.0f}      (target ~3,900)")
```
:::

## Part 3: Conditioning {#sec-conditioning}

We now condition the model on observed evidence. The key mechanical point: **replace `x = sample(...)` with `x = observe(x_val, ...)`**. Since `observe` returns the observed value, the rest of the model is unchanged. To ensure reusability, models are written to accept observed values as arguments.

### Task 5: Forward prediction — age and healthcare costs {#sec-forward-prediction}

Age influences BMI, which in turn influences both diabetes risk and costs. By conditioning on a specific age we obtain a predictive distribution for costs at that age.

Write `@model swiss_health_age(A_val)` that takes a fixed age value as an argument and conditions on it. Then:

a. Run with $A_{\mathsf{val}} = 25$ and $A_{\mathsf{val}} = 65$ using 10,000 particles each. Plot the two predictive cost distributions side by side.
b. For each age, compute $\mathbb{E}[B]$ and $P(D=1)$. How do each of these impact cost?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Model.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def swiss_health_age(A_val):
    S = sample("S", dist.Bernoulli(0.24))
    A = observe(A_val, dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0/43.0))
    P = sample("P", dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42))
    eta_B = 25.0 + (-0.5) * S + 0.05 * A + (-0.3) * P
    B = sample("B", dist.Normal(eta_B, 3.8))
    eta_D = -9.6 + 0.15 * B + 0.07 * A
    D = sample("D", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(eta_D)))
    eta_C = 7.5 + 0.2 * S + 0.65 * D + 0.03 * B
    C = sample("C", dist.LogNormal(eta_C, 0.6))
```

The only change from `swiss_health` is replacing `sample("A", ...)` with `observe(A_val, ...)`. Since $A$ is a root, this adds the log-density $\log p_{\mathsf{Gamma}}(A_{\mathsf{val}})$ as an importance weight and fixes $A = A_{\mathsf{val}}$ for all downstream computations.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_age25 = swiss_health_age(25.0, num_particles=10_000)
result_age65 = swiss_health_age(65.0, num_particles=10_000)
```

---

**Part a.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, res, label in zip(
    axes,
    [result_age25, result_age65],
    ["A = 25", "A = 65"],
):
    C_vals = res["C"]
    ax.hist(C_vals.numpy(), bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.7)
    ax.axvline(C_vals.median().item(), color="red", linewidth=1.5,
               label=f"median = CHF {C_vals.median().item():,.0f}")
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_xlabel("Annual cost (CHF)")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 120_000)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

---

**Part b.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
E_B_25 = result_age25["B"].mean().item()
E_B_65 = result_age65["B"].mean().item()
P_D_25 = result_age25["D"].mean().item()
P_D_65 = result_age65["D"].mean().item()

print(f"         A=25    A=65")
print(f"E[B]:    {E_B_25:.2f}   {E_B_65:.2f}")
print(f"P(D=1):  {P_D_25:.3f}   {P_D_65:.3f}")
```

Both $\mathbb{E}[B]$ and $P(D=1)$ are higher at age 65 than at age 25. Higher BMI impacts cost directly via the $\gamma_B B$ term in the cost predictor, and indirectly via the $\gamma_D D$ term since higher BMI increases diabetes risk. In the updated model, age also has a direct effect on diabetes risk ($A \to D$), so the age-related increase in $P(D=1)$ is driven by both the indirect path $A \to B \to D$ (higher BMI at older ages) and the direct path $A \to D$.

:::

### Task 6: Backward inference — what does diabetes tell us about age? {#sec-backward-inference}

Information flows both ways in a probabilistic model. Observing that a variable takes a particular value can update our beliefs about its causes, not just its effects. Here, $D$ has $B$ as a parent and $B$ has $A$ as a parent, so conditioning on $D=1$ should alter our beliefs about $A$.

Write `@model swiss_health_diabetes(D_val)` that takes a diabetes observation as an argument and conditions on it. Then:

a. Run with $D_{\mathsf{val}} = 1$ using 20,000 particles. Compare the posterior distribution of $A$ to its unconditional distribution from Task 4. Why does observing diabetes shift beliefs about age?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Model.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def swiss_health_diabetes(D_val):
    S = sample("S", dist.Bernoulli(0.24))
    A = sample("A", dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0/43.0))
    P = sample("P", dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42))
    eta_B = 25.0 + (-0.5) * S + 0.05 * A + (-0.3) * P
    B = sample("B", dist.Normal(eta_B, 3.8))
    eta_D = -9.6 + 0.15 * B + 0.07 * A
    D = observe(D_val, dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(eta_D)))
    eta_C = 7.5 + 0.2 * S + 0.65 * D + 0.03 * B
    C = sample("C", dist.LogNormal(eta_C, 0.6))
```

The only change from `swiss_health` is replacing `sample("D", ...)` with `observe(D_val, ...)`. Since $D$ is not a root, each particle is weighted by the likelihood $P(D = D_{\mathsf{val}} \mid B)$.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_D1 = swiss_health_diabetes(1.0, num_particles=20_000)

print(summary(result_D1))
```

---

**Part a.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
A_prior = result["A"]
A_post  = result_D1["A"]

# Resample from the posterior using importance weights
weights = torch.softmax(result_D1.log_weights, dim=0)
idx = torch.multinomial(weights, 10_000, replacement=True)
A_post_resamp = A_post[idx]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.hist(A_prior.numpy(), bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.5,
        label=f"prior  mean={A_prior.mean():.1f}")
ax.hist(A_post_resamp.numpy(), bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.5,
        label=f"posterior | D=1  mean={A_post_resamp.mean():.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Age $A$ (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The posterior over $A$ shifts upward when we observe $D=1$. In the updated model, the reasoning runs backwards along two causal paths: the direct path $A \to D$ (age increases diabetes risk directly) and the indirect path $A \to B \to D$ (older age leads to higher BMI, which in turn increases diabetes risk). Both paths make older ages more credible when diabetes is observed, producing a stronger posterior shift than either path alone.
:::

### Task 7: Conditioning on BMI {#sec-see-vs-do}

$B$ is **not** a root: it depends on $S$, $A$, and $P$. Observing $B=32$ is therefore informative about the values of those variables.

Write `@model swiss_health_bmi(B_val)` that takes a fixed BMI value as an argument and conditions on it. Then:

a. Run with $B_{\mathsf{val}} = 32$ using 20,000 particles. Compare $P(S=1)$ in the posterior to its prior value $0.24$. Why does the posterior shift in the direction it does? Also plot the predictive distribution of $C$ and compare to the unconditional distribution from Task 4.

**Bonus.** Instead of conditioning on $B=32$, write a model that simply sets `B = 32.0` as a constant (no `sample`, no `observe`). Run with 10,000 particles and compare $P(S=1)$ to part a. What do you observe, and can you explain why the two approaches give different results?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

**Model.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def swiss_health_bmi(B_val):
    S = sample("S", dist.Bernoulli(0.24))
    A = sample("A", dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0/43.0))
    P = sample("P", dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42))
    eta_B = 25.0 + (-0.5) * S + 0.05 * A + (-0.3) * P
    B = observe(B_val, dist.Normal(eta_B, 3.8))
    eta_D = -9.6 + 0.15 * B + 0.07 * A
    D = sample("D", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(eta_D)))
    eta_C = 7.5 + 0.2 * S + 0.65 * D + 0.03 * B
    C = sample("C", dist.LogNormal(eta_C, 0.6))
```

The only change from `swiss_health` is replacing `sample("B", ...)` with `observe(B_val, ...)`. Since $\eta_B$ depends on $S$, $A$, and $P$, particles whose upstream values make $B_{\mathsf{val}}$ plausible receive higher weight, propagating the observation backwards.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
result_B32 = swiss_health_bmi(32.0, num_particles=20_000)

print(summary(result_B32))
```

---

**Part a.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
weights = torch.softmax(result_B32.log_weights, dim=0)
P_S1_post = (result_B32["S"] * weights).sum().item()
print(f"P(S=1) prior:           {0.24:.3f}")
print(f"P(S=1) | see(B=32):     {P_S1_post:.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
idx = torch.multinomial(weights, 10_000, replacement=True)
C_B32 = result_B32["C"][idx]
C_prior = result["C"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
ax.hist(C_prior.numpy(), bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.5,
        label=f"unconditional  median=CHF {C_prior.median().item():,.0f}")
ax.hist(C_B32.numpy(), bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.5,
        label=f"see(B=32)  median=CHF {C_B32.median().item():,.0f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Annual cost (CHF)")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_xlim(0, 120_000)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The posterior probability of smoking decreases because $B=32$ (overweight) is harder to reconcile with smoking, which lowers BMI. This lower smoking posterior feeds into costs via the direct edge $S \to C$, partially offsetting the higher cost prediction from $B=32$ itself.

---

**Bonus.**

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
@model
def swiss_health_do_bmi():
    S = sample("S", dist.Bernoulli(0.24))
    A = sample("A", dist.Gamma(6.0, 6.0/43.0))
    P = sample("P", dist.Gamma(1.60, 0.42))
    B = 32.0  # fixed constant — no sample, no observe
    eta_D = -9.6 + 0.15 * B + 0.07 * A
    D = sample("D", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(eta_D)))
    eta_C = 7.5 + 0.2 * S + 0.65 * D + 0.03 * B
    C = sample("C", dist.LogNormal(eta_C, 0.6))

result_do_B = swiss_health_do_bmi(num_particles=10_000)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
P_S1_do = result_do_B["S"].mean().item()
print(f"P(S=1) prior:           {0.24:.3f}")
print(f"P(S=1) | observe(B=32): {P_S1_post:.3f}")
print(f"P(S=1) | B=32 fixed:    {P_S1_do:.3f}")
```

When $B$ is fixed to $32$ as a constant, $S$, $A$, and $P$ are sampled freely from their prior distributions without any information from the value of $B$. In particular, $P(S=1)$ stays at its prior $0.24$, whereas conditioning on $B=32$ drives $P(S=1)$ below $0.24$ because high BMI is less consistent with smoking ($\alpha_S = -0.5$).
:::
